predictions.title: AMD's MI455X speedup claims shrink under independent benchmarking by Q4 2027
predictions.body: AMD's Advancing AI keynote converted its roadmap into shipping specs, and the headline was throughput. The Instinct MI455X, carrying 432GB of HBM4, was claimed to reach up to 34 times the token throughput of the prior MI355X; a ROCm update was claimed at 3.3 times the inference and 2.4 times the training performance of ROCm 7; and Helios was pitched at 30% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia's rack. Every one of those is a vendor figure measured under conditions AMD chose. An 'up to 34 times' token number rarely survives contact with a fixed workload, because it bundles a precision drop, the larger HBM4 capacity that lets bigger batches and models stay resident, and a favorable model-and-sequence mix, none of which a like-for-like comparison holds constant. The prediction is that when the MI455X and Helios reach independent, standardized benchmarking, an MLPerf Inference or Training round whose rules pin the model, precision and accuracy target regardless of who submits, or independent third-party throughput testing, the measured generational and software gains land well short of the announced multipliers, a fraction of the headline 34, 3.3 and 2.4 times, on matched workloads, by Q4 2027. The 30% tokens-per-dollar claim compresses further or stays unverifiable, because AMD disclosed no Helios list price, leaving the economic figure with no public denominator to check. The structural force is simply that standardized benchmarks fix the variables a keynote 'up to' number floats. What falsifies the call is a clean independent result, an MLPerf submission or a third-party measurement, reproducing the headline multipliers at or near their announced magnitude on like-for-like workloads before Q4 2027 closes.

reasoning.because: AMD's keynote claimed MI455X 34x tokens vs MI355X and ROCm 3.3x/2.4x over ROCm7, all vendor-measured
reasoning.given: Standardized benchmarks fix model, precision and accuracy — the variables a keynote number floats
reasoning.so_that: So independent MLPerf or third-party tests measure MI455X and ROCm gains well below the 34x, 3.3x and 2.4x headlines
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2027; MLPerf or third-party benchmark measures the like-for-like gap
reasoning.plain_language: AMD says its new chip is up to 34 times faster. When outsiders run fair, standard tests, the real gain will look much smaller.

predictions.summary: AMD's keynote claimed the MI455X hits up to 34x the MI355X's tokens and ROCm 3.3x/2.4x over ROCm 7, all vendor-measured. Standardized benchmarks fix model, precision and accuracy, so expect independent tests to land well below those headlines by Q4 2027.

predictions.title: Self-financed multi-decade power deals reach a second frontier lab by H2 2027
predictions.body: OpenAI's Project Camellia, unveiled July 22, is less notable for its size - a four-building Effingham County, Georgia campus drawing 3.2 gigawatts, backed by at least $20 billion and reported above $30 billion at full build - than for how the power is bought. OpenAI signed a 25-year supply agreement with Georgia Power, committed to pay the full cost of the electrical infrastructure so existing ratepayers are shielded, and offered up to a gigawatt of flexible demand response to steady the regional grid. That is a frontier lab taking direct control of power procurement and financing the grid itself, not renting space and letting a utility carry the interconnection. The prediction is that this structure - a multi-decade direct utility supply agreement, plus lab-funded electrical infrastructure, plus an explicit ratepayer-protection or demand-response commitment, at gigawatt scale - stops being an OpenAI signature and becomes the template a second named frontier-scale operator publicly adopts by H2 2027. The forcing function is stated in the news itself: grid interconnection, not GPU supply, is now the binding constraint on frontier-scale compute, and the queue for large-load hookups runs years. A lab that will not wait, and that faces regulators increasingly unwilling to let data centers shift transmission costs onto households, has to internalize the power problem - sign directly for decades of supply, pay for its own substations and lines, and offer the grid flexibility in return - exactly the concessions Camellia front-ran. Once one lab shows utilities and public-service commissions that shape of deal, it becomes the price of entry the next gigawatt campus is negotiated against. The prediction is falsified if, through H2 2027, no other frontier operator - among Anthropic, xAI, Meta, Google or a named Stargate-class competitor - discloses a gigawatt-scale campus under a multi-year direct utility supply agreement in which the lab funds its own grid interconnection and accepts a ratepayer-shield or large-scale demand-response term, and such self-financed power structures remain particular to OpenAI while peers keep buying conventional grid-supplied capacity or short renewable offtake.

reasoning.because: OpenAI's Camellia signs a 25-year Georgia Power deal and self-funds the grid to shield ratepayers
reasoning.given: Grid interconnection, not GPUs, is the binding constraint; regulators resist shifting costs to homes
reasoning.so_that: A second named frontier lab discloses a gigawatt campus on a multi-decade direct utility deal it funds the grid for
reasoning.landing: by H2 2027; a named lab (Anthropic, xAI, Meta, Google) discloses the deal
reasoning.plain_language: Getting electricity, not chips, now limits AI. So OpenAI signed a 25-year power deal and paid for the grid itself. Other labs will copy it.

predictions.summary: OpenAI's Camellia pairs a 3.2-gigawatt Georgia campus with a 25-year utility deal, lab-funded grid infrastructure shielding ratepayers, and demand response. Because grid interconnection now binds frontier compute, a second frontier lab should disclose the same self-financed structure by H2 2027.

predictions.title: Moonshot's chip-export exposure draws a filed US enforcement action by H1 2027
predictions.body: The White House's July 23 accusation against Moonshot AI fused two charges that look alike but rest on unequal legal ground. One is a model-weight-provenance claim: that Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable to build Kimi K3. The other is a chip-export claim: that it trained on export-banned Nvidia GB300 servers reached through Thailand to skirt controls. The prediction turns on the asymmetry between them. By H1 2027 the chip-export half converts into at least one concrete, publicly filed US enforcement action — an addition to the Commerce Department's Entity List, a documented export-control or transshipment enforcement measure, or a sanctions designation — that names Moonshot AI or targets the Thailand diversion route the administration cited; while the distillation half produces no comparable binding US legal penalty tied to the alleged Fable-to-K3 copying, staying an accusation, an intellectual-property or terms-of-service dispute, or a voluntary lab access-control response. The structural reason is that only one track has an enforcement instrument behind it. Export control is mature machinery: the Commerce Department already runs an Entity List, and the enforcement playbook for advanced-chip diversion through Southeast Asian intermediaries — built over the prior two years — is one this accusation slots directly into. Model-weight distillation has no equivalent statute: obtaining a model's outputs through its public interface and training on them is, at most, a contract or terms-of-service violation, not an export crime or a sanctionable act, and the administration itself has not detailed how it concluded K3 was distilled, a gap independent researchers pressed given Fable was public only since July 1. Enforcement flows to the track that carries a legal instrument. The call falsifies in either direction: it fails if, by H1 2027, no publicly filed US export action names Moonshot AI or the cited Thailand route and the chip charge stays purely rhetorical; and it fails equally if the US instead lands a binding penalty — a filed action, a sanction, or a new rule — that treats the alleged model distillation itself as the sanctionable act, showing the provenance track grew enforcement teeth after all.

reasoning.because: White House fused a chip-export charge (GB300 via Thailand) with a model-distillation charge
reasoning.given: Export control is a mature enforcement instrument; model-distillation has no equivalent statute
reasoning.so_that: The chip-export half becomes a filed US enforcement action while the distillation half draws no binding legal penalty
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; a filed US export action names Moonshot or the Thailand route
reasoning.plain_language: The US can punish Moonshot for sneaking banned chips through Thailand, but has no law against copying an AI's answers, so only chips get penalized.

predictions.summary: The White House's July 23 accusation fused a chip-export charge (Nvidia GB300 via Thailand) with a Fable-to-K3 distillation charge. Because only export control carries a statute, the prediction is the chip half becomes a filed US enforcement action naming Moonshot or the Thailand route by H1 2027.
